data.name: SpectraHubChartContinuumRemovalLabel1
data.value:
Continuum removal is a spectral analysis technique used to isolate absorption features in a spectrum by removing its overall shape or continuum. This process enhances the visibility of specific spectral characteristics, making it easier to analyze and compare different materials or substances. It is commonly applied in remote sensing and laboratory spectroscopy to improve the identification and classification of elements based on their unique absorption patterns.
HyperLab provides users with an intuitive and user-friendly interface for performing continuum removal, allowing them to precisely define the segments where this operation should be applied. The process is designed to be straightforward and accessible: users can interact directly with the chart by selecting specific points that define the desired segments for continuum removal. Once these points are chosen, HyperLab enables users to select the appropriate mathematical fit function for each segment, ensuring accurate correction of the spectral baseline.
The Core mode is ideal for quick and straightforward segment creation, making it accessible even to users who are new to the process. By simply selecting individual points, the system automatically generates segments.
The Pro mode offers advanced customization, making it particularly useful for precise spectral adjustments. Since each selected point defines an interval with adjustable boundary points, users can fine-tune the segments and apply the most appropriate approximation function for each case.

data.name: SpectraHubChartAlignmentLabel1
data.value: For users working with RAW spectra and for HyperLab’s scientific team preparing data for broader dissemination, a dedicated feature is available: spectral alignment.</br>This functionality originates from acquisition setups used at SLab: the spectrometer includes three internal detectors covering the following wavelength ranges (nm): 350-1000; 1000-1800; 1800-2500.</br>During measurements, the ratio between sample and reference signals can introduce discontinuities at the detector transition points, resulting in artificial misalignments in reflectance intensity.</br>To ensure high-quality data and streamline processing, HyperLab provides an automated correction function that resolves these misalignments, following the approach successfully implemented at SLab

data.name: SpectraHubChartContinuumRemovalCoreModeExplanation
data.value: Core mode is a fast method for defining segments used to remove the continuum. Each time a point on the aligned spectrum is clicked, a new point is added to the graph. Every pair of points defines a segment, which is displayed on the graph and listed as an item in the right-hand panel. For each segment, the fitting function applied to the corresponding portion of the spectrum can be modified. By default, a straight line is selected, but other fitting functions are also available

data.name: SpectraHubChartContinuumRemovalProModeExplanation
data.value: Pro mode is a more sophisticated and versatile system for defining segments used to remove the continuum. When clicking on a point in the aligned spectrum, two additional points are automatically created on either side of the selected point. These define a range within which a relative maximum is searched. This maximum is then used as an endpoint for the two segments it belongs to. Various approximation functions can be applied to the range, each potentially returning different relative maxima depending on the method used

data.name: SpectraHubChartSmoothingLabel1
data.value: HyperLab provides flexible smoothing options through the Savitzky-Golay algorithm. At the outset, users can choose to apply the algorithm either to the entire spectrum or to a set of three predefined segments, which are fully customizable. If the segmented approach is selected, users can adjust the number of segments as well as define their specific boundaries. For each segment—or for the whole spectrum—two essential parameters must be set: the window size, which determines the range of data points utilized in the smoothing process, and the polynomial order, which controls the degree of the polynomial fit. This setup allows researchers to fine-tune the smoothing process to the specific characteristics of their spectral data

data.name: SpectraHubChartBandAnalysisLabel1
data.value: HyperLab incorporates an advanced band analysis feature that can be applied to each spectral band corresponding to the segments defined during the continuum removal process. By simply pressing a button on the left sidebar, users can initiate the calculation of key parameters—band depth, band area, full width at half maximum (FWHM) and the wavelength of the band center. This parameters are mainly calculating following the approach described in Clark 1984. As the computations progress, the results are dynamically displayed on the graph, with the affected band, its FWHM, and the band center highlighted.

data.name: SpectraHubChartLegendExplanation1
data.value: The legend is used to display all spectra available for visualization on the chart page. Spectra are organized according to a parent-child relationship: each level results from processing the previous one, forming a hierarchical structure. This relationship is represented as a tree diagram, where the base level (e.g., raw or aligned) is the starting point, and all subsequent processing levels branch out from it.

data.name: SpectraHubChartLegendExplanation2
data.value: Each spectrum is shown with a colored square followed by its name and processing level. The color of the square corresponds to the spectral type, as explained in the color guide section. The square also indicates the visibility status of the spectrum:

data.name: SpectraHubChartLegendExplanation3
data.value:
• A fully colored square means the spectrum is visible.
  • A semi-transparent square means the spectrum is hidden.

data.name: SpectraHubChartLegendExplanation4
data.value: Visibility is automatically adjusted during processing to enhance clarity and prevent overcrowding. However, users can manually toggle visibility by clicking on the square.

data.name: SpectraHubSimpleSearchExplanation1
data.value: The simple search allows users to query the database using only one parameter at a time, selected from the available options: filename, sample name, material (rock or mineral name), origin type, or mineral type. When a user clicks on a search category—either to enter a value in a text field or to choose from a dropdown list—the selected category is automatically set as the current search type. This ensures that each search is focused and based on a single criterion, making the process intuitive and streamlined.

data.name: SpectraHubSimpleSearchExplanation2
data.value: A special note applies to the Search by material field, which enables users to find spectra based on the minerals, rocks, or meteorites that make up the examined sample. Users can begin typing the name of a material—such as a rock, mineral, or meteorite—and once at least three characters have been entered, pressing Enter will trigger the system to suggest matching names. These suggestions are grouped by category, making it easier to identify the desired material. Once selected, users can click the search button to retrieve the corresponding spectra.

data.name: SpectraHubSearchCommonExplanation
data.value: The system also offers an option to request spectra obtained from either single acquisitions or averaged acquisitions. Some spectra in the database result from a single measurement, while others are derived from multiple acquisitions that have been averaged to reduce potential noise. This distinction allows users to choose between raw data and more refined spectral profiles, depending on their analytical needs.

data.name: SpectraHubComplexSearchExplanation1
data.value: Complex searches use the same parameters available in simple searches—filename, sample name, material, origin type, and mineral type—but with enhanced flexibility. In this mode, users can input multiple values for each parameter and combine different parameters together in a single query. This allows for more refined and targeted results, making it easier to explore specific subsets of data based on multiple criteria simultaneously.

data.name: SpectraHubComplexSearchExplanation2
data.value: The complex search screen is divided into two main areas: on the left side, users will find buttons corresponding to the available search parameters, while the remaining space displays either an explanatory image illustrating how to build a search or, if available, a list of previously saved searches.

data.name: SpectraHubComplexSearchExplanation3
data.value: Once the complex search mode is activated, creating a new search is simple—just click one of the parameter buttons on the left. This action automatically generates a form for the selected field, along with a header. On the left side of the header are buttons to execute, save, or delete the search; on the right side, there is an additional button to remove the search form entirely.

data.name: SpectraHubComplexSearchExplanation4
data.value: Once a group is created, its corresponding button is grayed out and disabled to prevent the same group from being added multiple times to the search.

data.name: SpectraHubComplexSearchExplanation5
data.value: In complex searches, each search parameter can accept one or more values, which are linked together using a Boolean operator—AND or OR. This set of values forms what is referred to as a group. Multiple groups can be created within a single complex search, and these groups themselves can be connected using Boolean operators. This layered structure allows users to build highly customized queries by combining different criteria and logical relationships.

data.name: SpectraHubLoadLocalFiles4
data.value: Spectra uploaded from local files must be saved through the web app in order to be used on the Chart page. If the user is logged in, the uploaded files are stored in the central database, ensuring persistent access across sessions and devices. If the user is not logged in, the spectra are saved locally within the web app's storage, meaning they are only available on the current device and session.

data.name: SpectraHubLoadLocalFiles1
data.value: The upload panel includes two primary buttons: "Load SLab Spectra" and "Load External Spectra." The first button enables users to upload spectral data generated by SLab and stored locally on their device. This is particularly useful for integrating lab-generated results directly into the HyperLab environment. The second button allows users to import spectra from external sources, such as third-party databases or collaborative research files.

data.name: SpectraHubLoadLocalFiles3
data.value: Supported file formats include CSV and XML, provided they adhere to the compatibility requirements of the HyperLab application. This flexibility allows researchers to work with a wide range of data sources while maintaining consistency across the platform.

data.name: SpectraHubLoadLocalFiles2
data.value: Both types of spectra—SLab and external—can be seamlessly saved to the HyperLab cloud, ensuring secure storage and easy access for future analysis. Once uploaded, the spectra become available for visualization and comparison on the Graphs page, where users can explore spectral features, overlay datasets, and perform detailed evaluations.
